Constructing a Song Lineup: Series 3 BUILD THE PERFORMANCE AND TEST THE LINEUP Now construct the actual lineup. Start by identifying the opener, development songs, emotional centre and finale. For a 10-minute performance, try: Strong opener — 3 minutes Contrasting song — 3 minutes Memorable finale — 4 minutes For a 30-minute Performance :Opening — 4 minutes Familiar song — 4 minutes Contrasting piece — 4 minutes Feature/solo — 5 minutes Reflective section — 4 minutes Build-up — 4 minutes Finale — 5 minutes For a 60-minute concert, think in larger sections: introduction, development, artistic or technical centre, emotional reset, final build and climax. Allow time for introductions, transitions, instrument changes and audience interaction. Then conduct the most important test: walk through the performance mentally and practically. Ask: Are the performers becoming tired? Does the next song make sense? Are there unnecessary tempo repetitions? Does the emotional story develop? Are the transitions smooth? Does the finale feel earned? As a music instructor, mentor and choir director, I believe a lineup must be achievable, not merely impressive on paper. Your songs are the building blocks. Context gives them purpose. Content gives them meaning. Patterns create coherence. Dynamics create movement. Transitions create continuity. “When context, content, pattern and dynamics work together, a lineup stops being a list and becomes a story told through sound.” — Victor Adenola #art #band #bands #choir #churchchoir #Composition #creativity #music #musicDirector #musicians #musicperformance #musicproduction #performance #performancetips #singer #singers #singersgospelSingers #songStructure #SongWriting #Victoradenola

Constructing a Song Lineup: Series 3 BUILD THE PERFORMANCE AND TEST THE LINEUP Now construct the actual lineup. Start by identifying the opener, development songs, emotional centre and finale. For a 10-minute performance, try: Strong opener — 3 minutes Contrasting song — 3 minutes Memorable finale — 4 minutes For a 30-minute Performance :Opening — 4 minutes Familiar song — 4 minutes Contrasting piece — 4 minutes Feature/solo — 5 minutes Reflective section — 4 minutes Build-up — 4 minutes Finale — 5 minutes For a 60-minute concert, think in larger sections: introduction, development, artistic or technical centre, emotional reset, final build and climax. Allow time for introductions, transitions, instrument changes and audience interaction. Then conduct the most important test: walk through the performance mentally and practically. Ask: Are the performers becoming tired? Does the next song make sense? Are there unnecessary tempo repetitions? Does the emotional story develop? Are the transitions smooth? Does the finale feel earned? As a music instructor, mentor and choir director, I believe a lineup must be achievable, not merely impressive on paper. Your songs are the building blocks. Context gives them purpose. Content gives them meaning. Patterns create coherence. Dynamics create movement. Transitions create continuity. “When context, content, pattern and dynamics work together, a lineup stops being a list and becomes a story told through sound.” — Victor Adenola #art #band #bands #choir #churchchoir #Composition #creativity #music #musicDirector #musicians #musicperformance #musicproduction #performance #performancetips #singer #singers #singersgospelSingers #songStructure #SongWriting #Victoradenola

Constructing a Song Lineup: Series 2 CONNECT PATTERNS, CONTRAST AND DYNAMICS. Once the context and message are clear, examine the musical patterns. Look at tempo, key, rhythm, style, instrumentation, vocal difficulty, song length and familiarity. Do not arrange five energetic songs simply because they are your favourites. Likewise, five slow songs can make even an excellent performance feel stagnant. Think in terms of energy movement: High → Medium → Low → High → Medium → Peak Or Moderate → High → Reflective → High → Explosive The exact pattern depends on the event, but the principle remains. Pattern creates expectation while contrast creates interest. Dynamics should also be considered beyond forte and piano. In lineup construction, dynamics represent the emotional and physical energy of the entire performance. A technically demanding song may need to be followed by something less demanding so singers or instrumentalists can recover. A quiet song may be deliberately positioned after an energetic one to create emotional space. Transitions are equally important. Decide whether songs will connect through a sustained chord, instrumental vamp, spoken introduction, silence, key change or immediate continuation. As a music producer and performance director, I have found that these details often determine whether a lineup feels professional or improvised. “If every song is treated like the climax, nothing feels like the climax.” — Victor Adenola #art #band #bands #choir #churchchoir #Composition #music #musicDirector #musicians #musicperformance #musicproduction #performance #performancetips #singer #singersgospelSingers #songStructure #SongWriting #Victoradenola
